title: Bonding & Structure (Extended)
description: Giant ionic lattices, ionic bonding beyond Group I/VII, double and triple covalent bonds, intermolecular forces, silicon dioxide and metallic bonding — the Extended tier of Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: The Giant Ionic Lattice
notes.body:
Extended tier expects you to DESCRIBE the structure of an ionic compound, not just state its properties.

📌 Definition
Ionic compounds form a **giant ionic lattice** — a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, held together by strong electrostatic forces acting in ALL directions (not just between one pair of ions).

🔑 Properties explained by the lattice
• HIGH melting and boiling points — the strong forces run throughout the whole lattice, so a large amount of energy is needed to overcome them.
• BRITTLE — when a layer of ions is struck and slides, ions of the SAME charge are brought side by side; they repel, and the crystal splits apart.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'strong ionic bonds between molecules'. There are no molecules in an ionic compound — write 'strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice'.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Regular 3D arrangement of + and − ions; forces act in all directions.
• Brittleness = like charges align after a layer slips → repulsion → shatter.

notes.heading: Ionic Bonding Beyond Group I/VII
notes.body:
Extended questions move past NaCl to metals and non-metals from other groups, and to comparing lattice strengths.

🔑 Group III and beyond
• Aluminium (2,8,3) loses 3 electrons → Al³⁺ (2,8).
• Balancing charges: Al³⁺ with O²⁻ needs 2 aluminium ions for every 3 oxide ions → Al₂O₃ (total charge: 2 × 3+ and 3 × 2− = 0). Each oxygen gains 2 of the 6 electrons given up by the two aluminium atoms.

🔑 Lattice strength and ionic charge
The greater the charges on the ions, the stronger the electrostatic attraction in the lattice, and the higher the melting point: MgO (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) melts at about 2850 °C, far above NaCl (Na⁺ and Cl⁻, 801 °C). Quote the ion charges in your explanation — that is where the mark is.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing AlO or AlO₃. Work from the charges: 3+ needs 2− partners in a 2:3 ratio.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Group III metals form 3+ ions; Group VI non-metals form 2− ions.
• Bigger ionic charges → stronger lattice → higher melting point.

notes.heading: Double and Triple Covalent Bonds
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• A **double bond** is TWO shared pairs of electrons (4 electrons) between the same two atoms.
• A **triple bond** is THREE shared pairs (6 electrons).

🔑 The Extended diatomic set
• **O₂**: each O (2,6) needs 2 electrons → the atoms share 2 pairs → O=O. Each oxygen also has 2 lone pairs, reaching 8 outer electrons.
• **N₂**: each N (2,5) needs 3 electrons → 3 shared pairs → N≡N. Each nitrogen keeps 1 lone pair. The triple bond is very strong, which is why N₂ is so unreactive.
• **CO₂**: C (2,4) needs 4 electrons and each O needs 2 → carbon forms a double bond with EACH oxygen → O=C=O, 4 shared pairs in total, no lone pairs on carbon.

💡 Worked Example — checking CO₂
Carbon's outer shell: 4 shared pairs = 8 electrons ✓. Each oxygen: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 8 ✓.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing CO₂ with single bonds and a lone pair on carbon — that leaves carbon on only 6 electrons. If an atom is short of a full shell, add another shared pair.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bonds an atom forms = electrons it needs: O needs 2 (double bond in O₂), N needs 3 (triple bond in N₂).
• Count every atom to 8 (or 2 for H) to check your diagram.

notes.heading: Extended Dot-and-Cross Set: C₂H₄ and CH₃OH
notes.body:
The Extended molecule list adds organic molecules. The method never changes: each atom forms as many bonds as the electrons it needs, then check every atom reaches a full shell.

🔑 Ethene, C₂H₄
Each C needs 4 bonds; each H needs 1. The four H atoms take one bond each (4 C–H bonds), leaving each carbon 2 bonds short → the two carbons share TWO pairs with each other: a C=C double bond. Total: 4 single C–H bonds + 1 C=C double bond = 6 bonding pairs.

🔑 Methanol, CH₃OH
Carbon (needs 4) bonds to 3 H atoms and 1 O atom; oxygen (needs 2) bonds to C and to the final H. So the chain is H₃C–O–H: 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond, 1 O–H bond = 5 bonding pairs. Oxygen also carries 2 lone pairs; carbon has none.

💡 Worked Example — electron count for CH₃OH
C: 4 bonding pairs = 8 ✓. O: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 8 ✓. Each H: 1 shared pair = 2 ✓.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Joining the last H to carbon instead of oxygen in CH₃OH — the 'OH' in the formula is the alcohol group, so the H belongs on the O.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Carbon always forms 4 bonds; if H atoms don't use them all, the carbons bond multiply to each other.
• In CH₃OH, oxygen forms exactly 2 bonds (C–O–H) and keeps 2 lone pairs.

notes.heading: Intermolecular Forces
notes.body:
Extended tier makes you EXPLAIN the properties of simple molecular substances — Core only asked you to state them.

📌 Definition
**Intermolecular forces** are the weak attractive forces BETWEEN molecules. They are far weaker than the covalent bonds WITHIN the molecules.

🔑 The explanation template (learn it)
'Simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points because only the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules need to be overcome — the strong covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken.'

🔑 The size trend
Intermolecular forces get STRONGER as molecules get larger, so melting and boiling points rise: down Group VII, F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ is a liquid and I₂ is a solid at room temperature. Bigger molecule → stronger forces between molecules → more energy to separate them.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the covalent bonds break when the substance boils' — that is the automatic fail. Boiling separates molecules; it does not split them.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Weak forces BETWEEN molecules; strong bonds WITHIN molecules.
• Larger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → higher melting/boiling point.

notes.heading: Silicon Dioxide, SiO₂
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Silicon dioxide (sand, quartz) is a **giant covalent** structure: every silicon atom is covalently bonded to 4 oxygen atoms, and every oxygen atom is bonded to 2 silicon atoms, in a continuous network with no separate molecules.

🔑 Properties from the structure
• VERY HIGH melting point (~1700 °C) — melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the network.
• HARD — the same 3D bonding resists scratching.
• Does NOT conduct electricity — no ions and no delocalised electrons.

🔑 The CO₂ contrast (a favourite Extended question)
Carbon and silicon are in the same group, yet CO₂ is a gas (simple molecules, weak intermolecular forces) while SiO₂ is a high-melting solid (giant covalent network). Same outer-electron count, completely different structure type — the formula tells you nothing until you know the structure.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Treating SiO₂ as a molecule and blaming 'strong intermolecular forces' for its high melting point. There are no SiO₂ molecules; melting breaks covalent bonds.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Each Si: 4 bonds. Each O: 2 bonds. No molecules, no free electrons.
• Structure type (giant covalent) explains high m.p., hardness and non-conduction.

notes.heading: Metallic Bonding
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A metal consists of a lattice of **positive metal ions** (cations) in fixed positions, surrounded by a **sea of delocalised electrons** — the outer electrons have left their atoms and move freely through the whole structure. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and this electron sea.

🔑 Properties explained
• CONDUCTS ELECTRICITY when solid AND molten — the delocalised electrons are free to move in every state and carry the current.
• Good thermal conductor — the mobile electrons also transfer kinetic energy quickly.
• MALLEABLE and ductile — layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the electron sea flows with them, so the attraction is never broken (unlike an ionic crystal, which shatters when like charges align).
• Generally HIGH melting points — the ion–electron attraction is strong and acts throughout the lattice.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying metals conduct 'because the ions move'. In a metal the positive ions stay fixed in the lattice; only the delocalised electrons flow. (It is IONIC compounds that conduct by moving ions — and only when molten or aqueous.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Structure = positive ion lattice + sea of delocalised electrons.
• Conduction and malleability both trace back to the mobile electron sea.

illustration.alt: Diagram of metallic bonding showing a regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons, with an arrow showing electrons flowing when a voltage is applied.
illustration.caption: The metallic bond is the attraction between the fixed positive ions and the mobile sea of delocalised electrons — which explains conduction and malleability.

flashcards.definition: A regular, repeating 3D arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions.
flashcards.example: NaCl — the strong forces throughout the lattice give it a high melting point (801 °C).

flashcards.definition: When a layer of ions slips, ions of the same charge end up side by side and repel, splitting the crystal.
flashcards.example: A salt crystal shatters when struck; a copper sheet only dents.

flashcards.definition: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ balance in a 2:3 ratio (2 × 3+ against 3 × 2−), giving Al₂O₃.
flashcards.example: Each Al (2,8,3) loses 3 electrons; each O (2,6) gains 2 — two Al supply exactly three O.

flashcards.definition: The greater the charges on the ions, the stronger the electrostatic attraction in the lattice and the higher the melting point.
flashcards.example: MgO (Mg²⁺, O²⁻) melts at about 2850 °C; NaCl (Na⁺, Cl⁻) at 801 °C.

flashcards.definition: Two shared pairs of electrons (4 electrons) between the same two atoms.
flashcards.example: O=O in oxygen and the C=C bond in ethene; CO₂ has two double bonds, O=C=O.

flashcards.definition: Three shared pairs of electrons (6 electrons) between the same two atoms.
flashcards.example: N≡N in nitrogen — so strong that N₂ is very unreactive.

flashcards.definition: Each carbon forms 4 bonds: two C–H bonds and a C=C double bond shared between the carbons (6 bonding pairs in total).
flashcards.example: Dot-and-cross check: each C sees 8 outer electrons; each H sees 2.

flashcards.definition: Bonded as H₃C–O–H: 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond and 1 O–H bond; oxygen carries 2 lone pairs.
flashcards.example: 5 bonding pairs in total; the final H is on the oxygen, not the carbon.

flashcards.definition: Weak attractive forces BETWEEN molecules in simple molecular substances — much weaker than the covalent bonds within the molecules.
flashcards.example: Boiling water overcomes the forces between H₂O molecules; the O–H bonds are untouched.

flashcards.definition: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them — melting and boiling points rise with molecule size.
flashcards.example: F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ a liquid and I₂ a solid at room temperature.

flashcards.definition: A giant covalent network in which each Si is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O to 2 Si atoms — hard, very high melting point, non-conductor.
flashcards.example: Sand (SiO₂) melts around 1700 °C because melting breaks strong covalent bonds throughout the network.

flashcards.definition: The strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons that move freely through it.
flashcards.example: Copper conducts when solid (electrons flow) and is malleable (ion layers slide while the electron sea keeps them attracted).

choices: The attraction between two non-metal nuclei
The strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
The attraction between oppositely charged ions only
A weak force between neighbouring atoms
questions.explanation: In a metal the outer electrons are delocalised and move freely around a lattice of positive ions; the attraction between the ions and this electron sea is the metallic bond.

questions.stem: Which molecule contains a triple covalent bond?
choices: O₂
CO₂
N₂
Cl₂
questions.explanation: Each nitrogen (2,5) needs 3 electrons, so the two atoms share 3 pairs — N≡N. O₂ has a double bond, CO₂ has two double bonds, and Cl₂ has a single bond.

questions.stem: Silicon dioxide, SiO₂, is best described as:
choices: A giant covalent structure
A simple molecular substance
An ionic lattice
A metallic lattice
questions.explanation: In SiO₂ every silicon is covalently bonded to 4 oxygens and every oxygen to 2 silicons — a continuous giant covalent network with no separate molecules, unlike CO₂.

choices: Strong bonds within each molecule
Forces between oppositely charged ions
Forces between positive ions and delocalised electrons
Weak attractive forces between molecules
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces act BETWEEN molecules and are much weaker than the covalent bonds within them — overcoming them explains the low melting points of simple molecular substances.

questions.stem: How many electrons does each aluminium atom (2,8,3) lose when it forms an aluminium ion, Al³⁺?
questions.explanation: Aluminium loses its whole outer shell — all 3 outer electrons — to reach the configuration 2,8, forming Al³⁺. In Al₂O₃, two aluminium atoms supply the 6 electrons that three oxygen atoms need.

questions.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in an oxygen molecule, O₂?
questions.explanation: Each oxygen (2,6) needs 2 electrons to complete its shell, so the atoms share 2 pairs — a double bond, O=O. Each oxygen also keeps 2 lone pairs, reaching 8 outer electrons.

questions.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in TOTAL in a carbon dioxide molecule, CO₂?
questions.explanation: Carbon needs 4 electrons and each oxygen needs 2, so carbon forms a double bond with each oxygen — O=C=O is 2 double bonds = 4 shared pairs in total.

questions.stem: Why does an ionic crystal shatter when it is struck, rather than bending?
choices: The bonds in the lattice are too weak to hold it together
When a layer of ions slips, ions of the same charge are brought side by side and repel, splitting the crystal
The delocalised electrons escape from the lattice
The lattice melts under pressure
questions.explanation: In the regular lattice every ion is surrounded by opposite charges. A slipped layer aligns like charges (+ next to +, − next to −); the repulsion between them forces the crystal apart — brittleness.

questions.stem: In which state(s) does a metal conduct electricity?
choices: Both solid and molten
Only when molten
Only when dissolved in water
It never conducts
questions.explanation: The delocalised electrons are free to move in every state, so metals conduct when solid AND molten — unlike ionic compounds, which conduct only when molten or aqueous.

questions.stem: In an ethene molecule, C₂H₄, how many electrons are shared between the two carbon atoms?
questions.explanation: Each carbon forms 2 C–H bonds, leaving each 2 bonds short of its 4 — so the carbons share 2 pairs with each other: a C=C double bond, which is 4 shared electrons.

questions.stem: Metals are malleable but ionic crystals are brittle. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Metals have weaker bonds, so they deform more easily
Ionic bonds are strong in all directions, so the crystal cannot change shape
Metals contain no charged particles, so nothing repels
Layers of positive metal ions can slide while the sea of delocalised electrons keeps them attracted; in an ionic lattice a slipped layer aligns like charges, which repel
questions.explanation: The electron sea moves with the sliding ion layers, so the metallic attraction survives the shift. In an ionic lattice the same shift brings like charges together and the repulsion splits the crystal.

questions.stem: At room temperature Cl₂ is a gas, Br₂ is a liquid and I₂ is a solid. What explains this trend down Group VII?
choices: The molecules get larger down the group, so the intermolecular forces between them get stronger and more energy is needed to separate them
The covalent bonds get stronger down the group
Iodine is ionic while chlorine is covalent
Heavier atoms are harder to melt
questions.explanation: All three are simple molecular; the state change reflects how hard it is to separate the molecules. Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so boiling points rise down the group. The covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken on boiling.

questions.stem: In a dot-and-cross diagram of methanol, CH₃OH, how many bonding pairs are there in total, and how many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom?
choices: 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair
5 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
5 bonding pairs and no lone pairs
6 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
questions.explanation: The structure is H₃C–O–H: 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond and 1 O–H bond = 5 bonding pairs. Oxygen has 6 outer electrons of its own; 2 are used in bonding, leaving 4 as 2 lone pairs. Check: C sees 8, O sees 8, each H sees 2.

questions.stem: Carbon and silicon are in the same group, yet CO₂ sublimes at −78 °C while SiO₂ melts at about 1700 °C. Why are their properties so different?
choices: SiO₂ contains metallic bonding between silicon atoms
CO₂ is an ionic compound
CO₂ is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces between molecules, while SiO₂ is a giant covalent network in which melting must break strong covalent bonds
Silicon atoms are heavier than carbon atoms
questions.explanation: The group tells you the outer electrons, not the structure type. CO₂ forms small discrete molecules needing little energy to separate; SiO₂ forms a continuous covalent network whose bonds must be broken throughout — hence the enormous difference in melting point.

questions.stem: How many electrons in total are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
questions.explanation: Each nitrogen needs 3 electrons, so the atoms share 3 pairs — a triple bond, N≡N — which is 6 shared electrons. The strength of this bond is why N₂ is so unreactive. Choice 3 counts pairs, not electrons.
